sections.en: Rabbi Yehuda said: Rabbi Yishmael asked Rabbi Yehoshua a series of questions while they were traveling along the road. Rabbi Yishmael said to him: For what reason did the Sages prohibit the cheeses of gentiles? Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: Because gentiles curdle cheese with the stomach contents of an unslaughtered animal carcass, and as the carcass of an unslaughtered animal is not kosher, cheese that is curdled with it is likewise prohibited. In response, Rabbi Yishmael said to him: But aren’t the stomach contents of a burnt-offering subject to a more stringent prohibition than the stomach contents of an unslaughtered animal carcass? And yet they said: A priest who is open-minded [shedato yafa] with regard to what he eats may swallow [shorefah] the stomach contents of a burnt-offering while they are raw, and the other Sages did not agree with him. But the Sages said: One may not derive benefit from the stomach contents of a burnt-offering ab initio, and if one did derive benefit from them, he is not liable for misusing consecrated property. According to both opinions, deriving benefit from the stomach contents of a burnt-offering is not prohibited by Torah law. Since the halakha with regard to a burnt-offering is more stringent than that of an animal carcass, why would deriving benefit from the carcass be prohibited, while deriving benefit from the burnt-offering is permitted? Rabbi Yehoshua said to Rabbi Yishmael: The cheese of gentiles is prohibited because they curdle it in the stomach contents of calves used for idol worship. Since it is prohibited to derive benefit from such calves, cheese curdled in their stomach contents is also prohibited. Rabbi Yishmael said to him: If that is so, why didn’t the Sages prohibit deriving any benefit from the cheese, instead of merely prohibiting its consumption? Instead of answering Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yehoshua diverted his attention to another matter and said to him: Yishmael, how do you read the following verse in the Song of Songs (1:2)? Do you read it as: For Your love [dodekha] is better than wine, or as: For your love [dodayikh] is better than wine? The first version, which is in the masculine form, would be a reference to God, whereas the second version, in the feminine, would be a reference to the Jewish people. Rabbi Yishmael said to him that it should be read in the feminine: For your love [dodayikh] is better than wine. Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: The matter is not so, as another verse teaches with regard to it: “Your ointments [shemanekha] have a goodly fragrance” (Song of Songs 1:3). This phrase, which appears in the next verse, is written in the masculine form, and therefore it is determined that the preceding verse can also be understood in the masculine form.
sections.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, שָׁאַל רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אֶת רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, כְּשֶׁהָיוּ מְהַלְּכִין בַּדֶּרֶךְ. אָמַר לוֹ, מִפְּנֵי מָה אָסְרוּ גְבִינוֹת הַגּוֹיִם. אָמַר לוֹ, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין אוֹתָהּ בְּקֵבָה שֶׁל נְבֵלָה. אָמַר לוֹ, וַהֲלֹא קֵבַת עוֹלָה חֲמוּרָה מִקֵּבַת נְבֵלָה, וְאָמְרוּ, כֹּהֵן שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ יָפָה, שׂוֹרְפָהּ חַיָּה. וְלֹא הוֹדוּ לוֹ, אֲבָל אָמְרוּ, אֵין נֶהֱנִין וְלֹא מוֹעֲלִין. חָזַר, אָמַר לוֹ, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין אוֹתָהּ בְּקֵבַת עֶגְלֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה. אָמַר לוֹ, אִם כֵּן, לָמָּה לֹא אֲסָרוּהָ בַהֲנָאָה. הִשִּׂיאוֹ לְדָבָר אַחֵר, אָמַר לוֹ, יִשְׁמָעֵאל אָחִי, הֵיאַךְ אַתָּה קוֹרֵא (שיר השירים א), כִּי טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן, אוֹ כִּי טוֹבִים דֹּדַיִךְ. אָמַר לוֹ, כִּי טוֹבִים דֹּדַיִךְ. אָמַר לוֹ, אֵין הַדָּבָר כֵּן, שֶׁהֲרֵי חֲבֵרוֹ מְלַמֵּד עָלָיו, לְרֵיחַ שְׁמָנֶיךָ טוֹבִים:

en: חִילְתִּית, חִלְתִּ׳ f. (see חֵילַת II) assa foetida, an umbelliferous plant used, as a resin or in leaves, for a spice and for medicinal purposes. 'Uktzin III, 5. Shabbat XX, 3 (140ᵃ) אין שורין את הח׳ וכ׳ (Mishnah ed. חִילְתִּין) you must not dissolve the resin of asa-foetida in warm water (on the Sabbath). Yerushalmi ib. XX, 17ᶜ bottom of page מי ח׳ a solution of &c. Ib. ח׳ עצמה וכ׳ asaf. itself is used in food for healthy persons. Chullin 58ᵇ (distinction between the medicinal properties of the gum and those of the leaves). Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 קורט של ח׳ tears of &c. (Arukh עלה וכ׳ leaves). Sifré Devarim section (Parashah) 107; and from

חֵילֶק I, חֵלֶק m. ḥelek, name of a small fish preserved in brine, ḥelek-brine. [Latin: alec, alex, halec, allec, the variations indicating foreign origin; compare חֶילְקָא II.] Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 (Mishnah Nap. חלק). Ib. 39ᵃ, explained סוּלְתָּנִית. Ib. 34ᵇ ח׳ אומן ḥelek-brine prepared by a professional man.

חָלַב (denominative of חָלָב) to milk; to yield milk. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6, see חָלָב. Bekhoroth 20ᵇ רוב … חוֹלְבוֹת וכ׳ the majority of animals secrete no milk unless they have given birth; and from

Nifal - נֶחֱלַב to be milked. Shabbat 53ᵇ לֵיחָלֵב when the bag is tied on for milking purposes (to support the udders), opposed ליבש for drying up.

חָלָב, חֲלֵב (Biblical Hebrew) [secretion,] milk. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 ח׳ שחֲלָבוֹ וכ׳ milk (of a cow) milked by a gentile. Makhshirin VI, 5 מי ח׳ serum of milk; and from—בשר בח׳ the boiling of meat with milk, the prohibitory law concerning &c. (Shemot XXIV, 19; XXXIV, 26; Devarim XIV, 21). Pesachim 54ᵇ, see חִידּוּשׁ.—Chullin 110ᵃ לא גמירי דב׳ בח׳ אסור they did not know that boiling meat with milk was forbidden; and from—חֲלֵב בֵּיצִים white of eggs. Yerushalmi Terumot X, 47ᵇ bottom of page, compare חֶלְבּוֹן.—נֵץ (ה)ח׳ ornithogalum, Star of Bethlehem, a bulbous plant. Sheviit VII, 1, see חֶלְבֵּצִין; 'Uktzin III, 2.—Transferred הח׳ white wine. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 98, opposed אדום.

טָרִית f. (נטר, compare אִטְּרִי) preserve, pickle, especially salted or pickled fish. Megillah 6ᵃ טמוני זו ט׳ ‘stored things’ (Devarim XXXIII, 19) refers to tarith (as a valuable article of commerce); Sifré Devarim 354; Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 13.—Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 ט׳ טרופה brine containing hashed tarith (when you cannot recognize the clean and unclean fish). Ib. ט׳ שאינה טרופה in which the fish can be recognized. Nedarim VI, 4 he who vows abstinence from ‘fish’ מותר בט׳ טרופה is permitted to partake of hashed t. Berakhot 44ᵃ

טָרַף (Biblical Hebrew; compare טָרַד) [to move with vehemence,]
1) to tear, prey. Vayikra Rabbah section (Parashah) 26 טוֹרֵף ואוכל tears in order to satisfy his appetite. Kohelet Rabbah to X, 11 הארי ט׳ the lion goes out for prey. Sotah 47ᵇ טוֹרְפֵי טֶרֶף those robbing (the poor). Zevachim 53ᵇ חלקו של טוֹרֵף the territory of the tearer (wolf = Benjamin, Breishit XLIX, 27). Bava Kamma 116ᵇ לטוֹרְפָהּ to plunder it; and from

—2) to cast with force, knock, strike against; to throw away, reject, eject. Chullin III, 3 טְרָפָהּ בכותל he cast or knocked the bird against the wall. Pesikta d'Rav Kahana R. section (Parashah) 11; Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 2 מגרשה אני טוֹרְפָהּ אני I will divorce her, I will cast her out (compare טָרַד).—Berakhot 5ᵇ טוֹרְפִין לו וכ׳ his prayer is thrown in his face (refused). Yerushalmi Yevamot XVI, 15ᵈ top טְרָפַנִי, see טָרַד.

—3) to seize forcibly. Yoma IV, 1 ט׳ בקלפי he took the ballot out with haste.—Esp. to seize for a debt. Bava Metzia 15ᵃ ובא ב"ח וטְרָפָהּ and a creditor of the previous owner came and seized it, see טִירְפָּא.

—4) to chop, hash, to beat, mix. Shabbat XIX, 2 ט׳ יין ושמן beat wine and oil; and e.—Part. pass. טָרוּף, f. טְרוּפָה. Ib. 38ᵃ בשר ט׳ chopped meat. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6, see טָרִית. Yerushalmi Niddah IV, 51ᵃ (of a foetus). Shabbat VIII, 5 (80ᵇ) ביצה ט׳ an egg beaten and mixed with oil; and from V. טָרוּף.

—5) to hackle, comb (flax or wool). Kilayim IX, 1. Yerushalmi Orlah III, 63ᵃ; Yerushalmi Ketubot VI, end, 31ᵃ צמר בכור שטְרָפוֹ wool of a first-born that has been hackled (and mixed up with, other wool).

—6) to scrape, scour, to plane. Makhshirin II, 4 הטוֹרֵף את גגו (Variant המטהר) if one scrubs his roof; Tosefta ib. I, 8.

—7) to make טְרֵפָה, to inflict an organic defect. Chullin 85ᵇ, sq. צא טְרוֹף go and maim the animal (before slaughtering it).

Nifal - נִטְרַף
1) to become t’refah. Ib. 9ᵃ, and e. במה נִטְרְפָה from what cause it became t’refah

—2) to be in disorder, a) (with דעה, or לב) to be confused, bewildered, not fully conscious. Yerushalmi Shabbat II, 5ᵇ bottom of page נִטְרְפָה דעתו של אבא my father’s mind is unclear; Sanhedrin 68ᵃ. Ib. 43ᵃ כדי שתִּטָּרֵף דעתו (not שתטרוף) that his (the culprit’s) consciousness may be benumbed; Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 10.—Ib. נ׳ לבו his mind becomes confused (from drinking); and from—b) (with שעה, of political disturbances) to be troubled. Sanhedrin 11ᵃ; Sotah 48ᵇ; Tosefta ib. XIII, 5 נטרפה (ה)שעה the political condition was too much troubled (persecutions prevailing). Yerushalmi Demai V, 24ᵈ bottom of page; and e.

Piël - טֵרֵף
1) to shake vehemently, constantly. Sukkah III, 9 כל העם מטָרְפִין בלולביהן ed. Yerushalmi (Mishnah ed. Pesachim מט׳את לול׳; ed. מנעועין) all the people shook their branches constantly (during the recitation at Hallel, contradistinguished to נענע).

—2) to unbalance (the mind, compare טִלְטֵל).—Part. pass. מְטוֹרָף. Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 10 לבו מ׳ וכ׳ his mind is disturbed and he talks improper things, see supra.

—3) to reject one’s petition, to refuse. Part. pass. מְטוֹרָף. Berakhot V, 5 שהוא מ׳ that he (the patient for whom prayer is said) is rejected (bound to die), opposed מקובל accepted.

—4) to disfigure, to make ungainly by spots, incisions &c., see טָרוּף). Part. pass. as ab. Kohelet Rabbah to X, 11 the serpent is asked מפני מה גופך מט׳ why has thy body been disfigured (see Breishit III, 14)?

—5) to cast about (a ship on high sea), see Hithpaël—Part. pass. as ab.; pl. מְטוֹרָפִים, מְטוֹרָפִין. Yevamot 47ᵃ, see סָחַף.

Hifil - הִטְרִיף
1) to become t’refah, to be afflicted with a fatal organic disease. Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 12, end; Shir HaShirim Rabbah to VI, 4; Pesikta d'Rav Kahana Vayhi p. 10ᵃ, and e. לא הִטְרִיפוּ the animals were found to be free from an organic disease.—[
2) (in later liter.) to declare t’refah.]

—3) (denominative of טֶרֶף) a) to cover with foliage. Yalkut Breishit 119, see רָטַב.—b) to sprout with moisture, be sappy. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 69 ה׳ מצות וכ׳ (Yalkut Judges 38 הפריח) sprouted with good deeds &c., see רָטַב.—[
4) to distribute food, see טָרָף.]

Hithpaël - הִיטָּרֵף, , Nithpa. נִיטָּרֵף to be tossed about, to be in a storm near the shore. Taanit III, 7 (19ᵃ) על הספינה המִיטָּרֶפֶת וכ׳ for a ship which is seen from the coast to be tossed about; Taanit 14ᵃ המְטוֹרֶפֶת (see supra; Arukh ed. Kohelet נִטְרֶפֶת Nif.). Tosefta Shabbat XIII (XIV), 11 נִיטָּרְפָה ספינה וכ׳ the ship has been thrown back several times (was prevented from landing by the breakers).

יִשְׂרָאֵל proper noun (Biblical Hebrew) Israel.
1) I. (Jacob), the patriarch. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 68 י׳ סבא the patriarch I. the patriarch I. (not the people); and from

—2) I., the people. Berakhot 6ᵃ; and from—שונאי י׳ the enemies of Israel, often euphem. for Israel. Ib. 32ᵃ נתמוטטו … של ש׳ י׳ the feet of Israel would totter (in judgment); and from—V. כְּנֶסֶת.

—3) י׳ (= בן י׳) an Israelite, a) one not belonging to the priestly or levitic tribe; b) a Jew, opposed נכרי, גוי. Gittin V, 8. Tosefta Kiddushin V, 3; and from—Tosefta Pirkei Avot Zar. III, 5, sq. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6; and from—בַּת י׳ an Israelitish woman. Tosefta l. common gender. 1; 3; and from—plural יִשְׂרְאֵלוֹת (opposed to כַּהֲנוֹת, לְוִיּוֹת). Tosefta Sanhedrin IV, 2.

סַלְקוּנְדְרִית, סַלְקוּנְרִית f. (preceding) מלח ס׳ lumpy salt (used by bakers), for which, it was believed, entrails of unclean animals were used as a condiment or to polish its surface. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 (35ᵇ) מלח ס׳ Manuscript Munich (Mishnah ed. סלקונטית; Bavli ed. שלקונדית; Yerushalmi ed. סלוקנרית; Hilkhot Rabbeinu Alfasi סלקונתית). Tosefta ib. IV (V), 12 מלח סלקונתית שחורה ed. Zuckermandel (see Tosefefta) (Variant של קינטית, oth. ed. סלקונט׳) black Salḳundre salt (prepared by pouring saline water over piles of burning wood, see Lübker Reallex. section (Parashah) see Salinae); לבנה … white Salḳ. salt; Yerushalmi ib. IV, end, 42ᵃ; Bavli ib. 39ᵇ. Ib. מאי מלח ס׳ מלח שכל סלקונדרי רומי אוכלין אותה (Arukh סלוקתי … בה) what is Salḳ. salt? A salt which all Roman siliginarii use at their meals (R. Niss. to Hilkhot Rabbeinu Alfasi: which all Roman nobles eat, i.e. those using fine bakery or confections).

פַּת common gender. (Biblical Hebrew; a piece of bread, in gen. bread, food, sustenance. Bava Metzia 107ᵇ פת שחרית breakfast. Ib. (reference. to Shemot XXIII, 25) זו פת במלח וכ׳ that is the morning bread with salt and a ladleful of water. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 והפת והשמן שלהן their (the gentiles’) bread and oil; ib. 36ᵃ פִּיתָּן ושמנן. Yoma 74ᵇ, see סַל. Horayot 13ᵇ פת שלא בשל וכ׳ bread not sufficiently cooked (baked). Ib. פת פחמין bread baked on coals. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 67 פִּיתְּךָ אפויה, see אָפָה; and from—[פת כומרין, see פַּתְכּוּמְרִין.]—plural פִּתִּים, פִּתִּין, פִּי׳ pieces. Menachot III, 2 או שפתתן פ׳ מרובות or if he broke them in too many (small) pieces; ib. 18ᵇ מאי פ׳ מרובות שריבה בפתיתין ‘many pieces’ means that he parted the pieces repeatedly; Sifra Vayikra, N’dab., Parah 10, Chaldaic XII (reference. to Vayikra II, 6) אותה לפ׳ ואין פִּתֶּיהָ לפ׳ thou shalt part it in pieces, but not its pieces again in pieces; Yalkut Vayikra 450, see פָּתִית.

צִיר I m. (צוּר; compare זוּרְיוֹן, זַיָּירָא) juice, brine. Sifra Sh’mini, Chaldaic IV, Parah 3 (reference. to Vayikra XI, 12) שקץ לאסור את צִירָן ורוטבן וכ׳ ‘abomination’ is used to imply the prohibition of their brine or soup &c. Ib. לאסור צִירָם ורוטבם. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 (35ᵇ) צ׳ שאין בה דגה (read בו) brine in which no fish is distinguishable. Ib. 40ᵃ בצירן in their brine (without the fish), opposed בגופן. Chullin 99ᵇ; and from

comments.en: קוֹרֶט m. (קדט, compare קָרַץ) a particle, grain, (coagulated) drop. Sanhedrin 43ᵃ, see לְבוֹנָה. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6, see חִילְתִּית. Menachot 11ᵃ ועמדה על ק׳ אחד so that only one grain of frankincense remained. Chullin 50ᵇ, sq. ק׳ דם a drop of coagulated blood; and from—plural קוֹרָטִין, קֳרָטִין, קֳרָטִים. Ib. 58ᵇ בק׳ concerning the tears of assafœtida, opposed to עלין leaves. Menachot l. common gender. Yerushalmi Shabbat III, end, 6ᶜ ק׳ של בוסם grains of burnt spices (remnants in the coal pan); Bavli Shabbat 47ᵃ דאית ביה ק׳ some grains were yet left in it. Ib. ק׳ בי רבי וכ׳ did those of the house of Rabbi care for the grains left unburnt? Tosefta Menachot I, 17; and from

שֶׁלֶק m. (preceding) seething, overboiled matter. Yerushalmi Sheviit VI, 36ᶜ top מי ש׳ של ביצים water in which eggs have been boiled; Yerushalmi Gittin I, 43ᶜ. Berakhot VI, 8 אפי׳ אכל ש׳ וכ׳ even if one eats overboiled vegetable, and he makes a meal of it. Ib. 44ᵇ ומי איכא מידי דהוי ש׳ מזונו (not מזוני) is there a thing which a person makes a meal of when it is boiled to a pulp?; and e.—plural שְׁלָקִין, שְׁלָקוֹת. Tosefta Terumot VII, 13; Y, ib. VIII, 45ᵈ. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 6 ש׳ וכבשין things preserved by boiling or by pressing (by gentiles); and e.

en: MISHNA: And these are permitted for consumption: Milk that was milked by a gentile and a Jew watched him doing so; and honey; and grape clusters [davdevaniyyot] which, despite the fact that they are dripping juice, are not subject to the halakhot of susceptibility to ritual impurity caused by contact with that liquid; and pickled vegetables whose usual manner of preparation does not involve adding wine and vinegar to them; and tarit fish that is not minced; and brine that has fish in it; and the leaf of a ḥiltit plant; and rolled olive cakes [geluskaot].

Rabbi Yosei says: Overripe olives are prohibited. Locusts that come from a salesman’s basket are prohibited, whereas those that come from the storeroom [heftek] are permitted; and likewise with regard to the portion of the produce designated for the priest [teruma], as will be explained in the Gemara.
he: מתני׳ ואלו מותרין באכילה חלב שחלבו עובד כוכבים וישראל רואהו והדבש והדבדבניות אע"פ שמנטפין אין בהן משום הכשר משקה וכבשין שאין דרכן לתת לתוכן יין וחומץ וטרית שאינה טרופה וציר שיש בה דגה ועלה של חילתית וזיתי גלוסקאות המגולגלין
ר' יוסי אומר השלחין אסורין החגבים הבאים מן הסלולה אסורין מן ההפתק מותרין וכן לתרומה:

sections.en: This mishna lists items belonging to gentiles which it is prohibited to consume, but from which it is permitted to derive benefit. And these are items that belong to gentiles and are prohibited, but their prohibition is not that of an item from which deriving benefit is prohibited: Milk that was milked by a gentile and a Jew did not see him performing this action, and their bread and oil. The mishna notes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court permitted the oil of gentiles entirely. The mishna resumes its list: And boiled and pickled vegetables, whose usual manner of preparation involves adding wine and vinegar to them, and minced tarit fish, and brine that does not have a kilbit fish floating in it, and ḥilak, and a sliver of ḥiltit, and salkondit salt (see 39b); all these are prohibited, but their prohibition is not that of item from which deriving benefit is prohibited.
sections.he: אֵלּוּ דְבָרִים שֶׁל גּוֹיִם אֲסוּרִין וְאֵין אִסּוּרָן אִסּוּר הֲנָאָה. חָלָב שֶׁחֲלָבוֹ גוֹי וְאֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל רוֹאֵהוּ, וְהַפַּת, וְהַשֶּׁמֶן שֶׁלָּהֶן. רַבִּי וּבֵית דִּינוֹ הִתִּירוּ בַשֶּׁמֶן. וּשְׁלָקוֹת, וּכְבָשִׁין שֶׁדַּרְכָּן לָתֵת לְתוֹכָן יַיִן וָחֹמֶץ, וְטָרִית טְרוּפָה, וְצִיר שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ דָּגָה כִלְבִּית שׁוֹטֶטֶת בּוֹ, וְהַחִלָּק, וְקֹרֶט שֶׁל חִלְתִּית, וּמֶלַח סַלְקוֹנְטִית, הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ אֲסוּרִין וְאֵין אִסּוּרָן אִסּוּר הֲנָאָה:

en:
גְּלוּסְקָא, קְלוּסְקָא, קין common gender. (a contraction of גלוסביקא or גלופסיקא, Lesbiacus, Lesbiaca, see כְּלוּפְסִין, לִבְסִים, קְלוּפְ׳, גְּלוּפְ׳; as to guttural before ל, see גְּלוּגְדְּקָא) relating to Lesbos (an island of the Aegean Sea, noted for its fertility and luxuries), Lesbian, whence
1) [in Syriac] name of a brand of white flour (Payne Smith, Thesaurus Syriacus 726), a white and delicate bread (compare Athenæus Deipnosophistæ III, 111). Tosefta Berakhot IV, 15 שלמה של גלוסקין an unbroken loaf of g’luskin, opposed של בע"הב home-made. Demai VI, 12 buy for me גְּלוּסְקָן אחד ed. (accus.; Manuscript Munich גלוסקא אחת, Arukh קין אחת …, Rabbenu Shimshon קלוסקן) one loaf &c. Yerushalmi Pirkei Avot Zar. I, 40ᵃ bottom of page קלוסקין אחת; Eruvin 64ᵇ גלוסקין plural—Pesachim 6ᵇ he may find ג׳ יפה ודעתו עליה Rashi (ed. ודעתיה עילויה, Manuscript Munich יפיפיה) a fine gl. which he may have the intention of eating (in place of burning). Eicha Rabbah to I, 16 גלוסקאן; and e.—plural גְּלוּסְקָאוֹת, גְּלוּסְקִין, קְלוּ׳. Shabbat 30ᵇ. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 88, beginning Eicha Rabbah to II, 12 גלו׳ (Arukh ed. Kohelet קלסקין); and e.

—2) a superior sort of olives already pressed when appearing in the market (θλασταί, σταφυλίδες, see Athenæus l. common gender. II, 56; compare כְּלוּפְסִין). Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7 זיתי קלוסקא המגולגלין Yerushalmi ed. II, 10 (Mishnah זתים גלוסקאות, Bavli ed. 39ᵇ זיתי ג׳, Mishnah Nap. קלוסטא, Arukh ed. Kohelet section (Parashah) see גלגל: קלוסטא, קלוסטרא). Bavli ib. 40ᵇ (ed. Pesachim and oth. קלוסקא, Hilkhot Rabbeinu Alfasi early ed. גלוסטא, see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 4). Yerushalmi ib. II, 42ᵃ bottom of page הן זיתי ק׳ וכ׳ zethé k’luska is the same as rolled olives. [Shemot Rabbah section (Parashah) 30 גלוסקאות, see גְּלוֹסְקְמָא.]

גְּמִי I, גְּמַע , Pa. גַּמֵּי, גַּמַּע Chaldaic = h. to swallow, quaff. Targum Job XXXIX, 30 גָּמְעָן (Manuscript גַּמְעַאן).—Yerushalmi Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 41ᶜ bottom of page (explained שורפה, Mishnah Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7) גמי לה (ed. גמילה, correct accordingly) he quaffs it, sucks it out. Sukkah 49ᵇ לִיגְמַע גַּמּוּעֵי let him quaff (take full draughts); ib. אגמע גמועי (read: מְגַמַּע with Rashi, or גַּמַּע, see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 300). Shabbat 109ᵇ וליגמע.

דַּבְּרָנִית f. (compare preceding) talkative, loquacious. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 18, beginning—plural דַּבְּרָנִיּוֹת. Berakhot 48ᵇ. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 45; Devarim Rabbah section (Parashah) 6; and e. [Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7, see דַּבְדְּבָנִיּוֹת].

דַּבְדְּבָנִיּוֹת f. plural (reduplic. of דבב) lumps of dripping grapes (exposed to heat; see דָּבַב). Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7 (39ᵇ) והדבד׳ (Mishnah ed. דברניות, Manuscript Munich דברבנ׳; Yerushalmi ed. דכדב׳, correct accordingly; Mishnah Nap. דַּמְדְּמָנִיּוֹת). Yerushalmi Shabbat I, 4ᵃ bottom of page; Yerushalmi Beitzah II, 62ᵃ top דמדמ׳. Cmp. אֲדַמְדְּמָנֵי.

הֶפְתֵּק m. (פתק to cut, divide off; Variant lect. see infra) the store-room in the dwelling house out of which the daily portions of provision and work are distributed; also the retailer’s shelves &c., contradistinguished to אוצר ware-house. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7 (39ᵇ) הבאין מן הה׳ the preserved locusts which the merchant takes from the shelves, contradistinguished to מן הסלולה, those laid out in baskets in front of the counter. Pirkei Avot Zar. 40ᵇ מן הה׳ מן האוצר ומן הספינה (not הסלולה, see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 5); Tosefta ib. IV (V), 12 מן הפתק וכ׳ ed. Zuckermandel (see Tosefefta) (Variant הפתיק, compare הֶמְסֵס for fusion of article) from the shelves, the ware-room or the ship.—Shabbat 50ᵃ; Tosefta ib. III (IV), 19 גיזי צמר של ה׳ cut wool stored in the pantry (intended for spinning; Rashi: from the merchant’s shelves). [Ar. section (Parashah) see אפתק reads: אוּפְתֵּק, noting a Variant ה׳. One Manuscript Arukh, and Mishnah ed. Nap. read אפותיק for אוּפְתֵּיק, induced by phonetic resemblance to ἀποθήκη. V. Arukh ed. Kohelet section (Parashah) see אפתק, and Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) to Pirkei Avot Zar. 39ᵇ note 8.]

סְלִילָה, סְלוּ׳ f. (denominative of סַל) the shopkeeper’s basket stand. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7 (39ᵇ) Yerushalmi ed. and Arukh (Bavli ed. and Mishnah הסלו׳), see הֶפְתֵּק; Tosefta ib. IV (V), 12 ed. Zuckermandel (see Tosefefta) (oth. ed. … לָא).—[Bab. ib. 40ᵇ מן הס׳ (twice), read הספינה, see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 5.].

comments.en: שֶׁלַח, שְׁלוּחַ) m. (שָׁלַח) [stripped of its skin,] a pressed olive the stone of which slips out at a touch.—plural שְׁלָחִין, שְׁלוּ׳. Pirkei Avot Zar. II, 7 (39ᵇ; Mishnah and Yerushalmi ed. שלו׳). Ib. 40ᵇ היכי דמי ש׳ וכ׳ when are they called Sh’laḥin? When the stone slips out as you take the olive in your hand.

en: MISHNA: This mishna lists items belonging to gentiles which it is prohibited to consume, but from which it is permitted to derive benefit. And these are items that belong to gentiles and are prohibited, but their prohibition is not that of an item from which deriving benefit is prohibited: Milk that was milked by a gentile and a Jew did not see him performing this action, and their bread and oil. The mishna notes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court permitted the oil of gentiles entirely.

The mishna resumes its list: And boiled and pickled vegetables, whose usual manner of preparation involves adding wine and vinegar to them, and minced tarit fish, and brine that does not have a kilbit fish floating in it, and ḥilak, and a sliver of ḥiltit, and salkondit salt (see 39b); all these are prohibited, but their prohibition is not that of item from which deriving benefit is prohibited.
he: מתני׳ ואלו דברים של עובדי כוכבים אסורין ואין איסורן איסור הנאה חלב שחלבו עובד כוכבים ואין ישראל רואהו והפת והשמן שלהן רבי ובית דינו התירו השמן
והשלקות וכבשין שדרכן לתת לתוכן יין וחומץ וטרית טרופה וציר שאין בה דגה כלבית שוטטת בו והחילק וקורט של חלתית ומלח שלקונדית הרי אלו אסורין ואין איסורן איסור הנאה:

comments.en: These are the “hides pierced at the heart” [which are mentioned in m. Avodah Zarah 2:3]: All that are perforated at its heart and made like a kind of aperture [in the roof looking to the ground floor]. But if it is straight, it is permitted. Preserved and boiled produce of idolators, into which it is customary to put wine and vineyard and Hadrianic earthenware, [they are subject to] a prohibition on benefit according to Rabbi Meir but the Sages say they are not subject to a prohibition on benefit. Pressed olives that are sold at the entrances to bathhouses are prohibited for eating and permitted for benefit. Rabbi Yosei prohibits them even for benefit because they pour vinegar on them in order to remove their pits.
comments.he: אלו הן עורות לבובין כל הקרוע כנגד לבן ועשה כמין ארובה אבל אם היה משוך הרי זה מותר הכבשין ושלקות של עובדי כוכבים שדרכן לתת בהן יין וחומץ וחרס הדריני אסור בהנאה דברי ר"מ וחכמים אומרים אין איסורן איסור הנאה זיתים השלחים הנמכרים על פתחי מרחצאות אסורים באכילה ומותרין בהנאה ר' יוסי אוסרן אף בהנאה מפני שמזלפין עליהן חומץ כדי שיהו חולצין את גרעיניהן.

sections.en: And these are permitted for consumption: Milk that was milked by a gentile and a Jew watched him doing so; and honey; and grape clusters [davdevaniyyot] which, despite the fact that they are dripping juice, are not subject to the halakhot of susceptibility to ritual impurity caused by contact with that liquid; and pickled vegetables whose usual manner of preparation does not involve adding wine and vinegar to them; and tarit fish that is not minced; and brine that has fish in it; and the leaf of a ḥiltit plant; and rolled olive cakes [geluskaot]. Rabbi Yosei says: Overripe olives are prohibited. Locusts that come from a salesman’s basket are prohibited, whereas those that come from the storeroom [heftek] are permitted; and likewise with regard to the portion of the produce designated for the priest [teruma], as will be explained in the Gemara.
sections.he: אֵלּוּ מֻתָּרִין בַּאֲכִילָה. חָלָב שֶׁחֲלָבוֹ גוֹי וְיִשְׂרָאֵל רוֹאֵהוּ. וְהַדְּבַשׁ. וְהַדַּבְדָּנִיּוֹת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּנַטְּפִין, אֵין בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם הֶכְשֵׁר מַשְׁקֶה. וּכְבָשִׁין שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן לָתֵת לְתוֹכָן יַיִן וָחֹמֶץ. וְטָרִית שֶׁאֵינָהּ טְרוּפָה. וְצִיר שֶׁיֶּשׁ בָּהּ דָּגָה. וְעָלֶה שֶׁל חִלְתִּית. וְזֵיתִים גְּלֻסְקָאוֹת הַמְגֻלְגָּלִין. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, הַשְּׁלוּחִין, אֲסוּרִין. הַחֲגָבִים הַבָּאִים מִן הַסְּלוּלָה, אֲסוּרִין. מִן הַהַפְתֵּק, מֻתָּרִין. וְכֵן לִתְרוּמָה:
